passage: Tuition notes, Friday. Written by Eshaan, maths tutor. Chinmay, ten, taught me something this month. Two weeks ago I solved a whole fraction sum for him on the board. Then: "Can I do the next one alone?"

Priscila, ten, wanted to bake bread for the school fair in Porto Alegre, and her neighbour Jana was a baker.
The first Saturday, Jana did it all, flour, kneading, shaping, while Priscila held the spoon. The loaf was perfect. Priscila said thank you in a very small voice and didn't want to carry it.
The next Saturday Jana had a delivery. "You watched me. Try the braided one," she said, and left. The dough stuck to everything, the braid fell apart, and Priscila sat on the floor and cried.
The third Saturday Jana stayed, hands in her apron pockets. "What comes next, do you think?" When the braid sagged, she only said, "Tighter at the top." Priscila's loaf came out lopsided. She carried it to the fair herself.

qa.q: What did Priscila do while Jana did everything on the first Saturday?
qa.a: She held the spoon.

qa.q: Why did Priscila say thank you in a very small voice after the first loaf?
qa.a: She felt small because the perfect loaf wasn't really hers, which is why she didn't want to carry it.

qa.q: What changed on the third Saturday that finally worked?
qa.a: Jana stayed close but kept her hands in her pockets, asking questions and giving one tip, so the task was hard but not hopeless.

qa.q: What might Jana have noticed about Priscila across the three Saturdays?
qa.a: That doing everything and doing nothing both left Priscila unhappy, while standing by let her feel proud enough to carry her own loaf.

grounding: A girl feels small when a baker does everything, gives up when left alone with a hard loaf, and grows when the baker stays near with only a hint.

Irawati, you're stuck on those fractions and asking me to just do them. Let me tell you about two teachers I had.
At ten, my tutor did every one of my sums. My homework was perfect. But in the exam I sat there like a stone. I felt so small, like everyone else knew a secret I'd never been told.
The next year, a new teacher gave us algebra and left the room. I looked at the page for an hour and gave up.
Then my aunt, Kusum Masi, started sitting next to me in the evenings. She never did a sum. She'd just say, "What do you know? What's the first step?" and wait.
I'm Sonali, your Nani. That's how I learned maths. Now, show me what you've tried.

It was hard. But I understood it.

Class teacher's note, Class 5

Sonali has been struggling with long division. Last week her tutor, Pradeep, did her homework with her by solving each question while she copied. She got full marks but could not do one sum in class. She looked down at her desk and said nothing.
The week before, a substitute had left her with a sheet far beyond her level. She put her head down and did not try.
This week I sat beside her. I asked what she had tried, then gave one hint about the first step. She did the rest, slowly. When she finished, she looked at me and smiled for the first time this term.
I have spoken with Pradeep about hints instead of answers.

qa.q: What did the note-writer do that helped Sonali learn?
qa.a: They sat beside her, asked what she had tried, and gave one hint, letting her do the rest herself.

qa.q: How might Pradeep's tutoring change after the talk?
qa.a: Pradeep may start giving hints instead of answers, helping Sonali learn rather than copy.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a child learning nothing from full solutions, giving up alone, and growing when guided with one hint.
